name: The privative theory of evil
plain_explanation: Boethius's idea that evil is not really a 'thing' in its own right, but simply a lack or absence of good -- the way darkness is not a substance but merely the absence of light.
precise_definition: The doctrine that evil has no positive existence but is merely a privation (deficiency) of good; since God, who is the chiefest good, can do everything, and God cannot do evil, evil must be nothing, i.e., not a positive reality God fails or refuses to produce.
why_it_mattered: It lets Boethius reconcile divine omnipotence and perfect goodness with the existence of apparent evil, and grounds his further claim that the wicked, lacking real being, are in fact weak, while the virtuous, possessing the good, are truly powerful.
historical_origin: Developed in the Consolation of Philosophy (524), in the Platonic metaphysical tradition of treating imperfection as a lack implying a perfect pattern.
examples: 'Can God do evil? No. Therefore evil is nothing, since God can do everything.'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Transmitted a broadly Platonic and Neoplatonic treatment of the problem of evil into medieval Christian philosophy.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Framed in explicitly theological terms (God's omnipotence and goodness) though argued in a Platonic philosophical idiom.
